entries.c8b6f23f81f541c04a4a08f3894e8287dd4e378d: <div sID="gen31967" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Phil.3" sID="Phil.3"/> <div eID="gen31967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31968" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31969" type="x-p"/> He cautions them against judaizing seducers (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.1-Phil.3.3">ver. 1-3</reference>) and proposes his own example: and here he enumerates the privileges of his Jewish state which he rejected (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.4-Phil.3.8">ver. 4-8</reference>), describes the matter of his own choice (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.9-Phil.3.16">ver. 9-16</reference>), and closes with an exhortation to beware of wicked men, and to follow his example, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.17-Phil.3.21">ver. 17-21</reference>.
entries.1f91b9b6ff5c5eceb48f2b72a5bfee9a00e38356: <div eID="gen31969" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31968" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Description of True Christians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31970" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you, to me indeed <hi type="italic">is</hi> not grievous, but for you <hi type="italic">it is</hi> safe. <hi type="super">2</hi> Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision. <hi type="super">3</hi> For we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh. <div eID="gen31970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31971" type="x-p"/> It seems the church of the Philippians, though a faithful and flourishing church, was disturbed by the judaizing teachers, who endeavoured to keep up the law of Moses, and mix the observances of it with the doctrine of Christ and his institutions. He begins the chapter with warnings against these seducers. <div eID="gen31971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31972" type="x-p"/> I. He exhorts them to <hi type="italic">rejoice in the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">v. 1</reference>), to rest satisfied in the interest they had in him and the benefit they hoped for by him. It is the character and temper of sincere Christians to rejoice in Christ Jesus. The more we take of the comfort of our religion the more closely we shall cleave to it: the more we rejoice in Christ the more willing we shall be to do and suffer for him, and the less danger we shalt be in of being drawn away from him. The <hi type="italic">joy of the Lord is our strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh. viii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen31972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31973" type="x-p"/> II. He cautions them to take heed of those false teachers: <hi type="italic">To write the same thing to you to me indeed is not grievous, but for you it is safe;</hi> that is, the same things which I have already preached to you; as if he had said, "What has been presented to your ears shall be presented to your eyes: what I have spoken formerly shall now be written; to show that I am still of the same mind." <hi type="italic">To me indeed is not grievous.</hi> Observe, 1. Ministers must not think any thing grievous to themselves which they have reason to believe is safe and edifying to the people. 2. It is good for us often to hear the same truths, to revive the remembrance and strengthen the impression of things of importance. It is a wanton curiosity to desire always to hear some new thing. It is a needful caution he here gives: <hi type="italic">Beware of dogs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.2">v. 2</reference>. The prophet calls the false prophets dumb dogs (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.10">Isa. lxvi. 10</reference>), to which the apostle here seems to refer. <hi type="italic">Dogs,</hi> for their malice against the faithful professors of the gospel of Christ, barking at them and biting them. They cried up good works in opposition to the faith of Christ; but Paul calls them evil workers: they boasted themselves to be of the circumcision; but he calls them the concision: they rent and tore the church of Christ, and cut it to pieces; or contended for an abolished rite, a mere insignificant cutting of the flesh. <div eID="gen31973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31974" type="x-p"/> III. He describes true Christians, who are indeed the circumcision, the spiritual circumcision, the peculiar of people of God, who are in covenant with him, as the Old-Testament Israelites were: <hi type="italic">We are the circumcision, who worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh.</hi> Here are three characters:—1. They worshipped in the spirit, in opposition to the carnal ordinances of the Old-Testament, which consist in meats, and drinks, and divers washings, &c. Christianity takes us off from these things, and teaches us to be inward with God in all the duties of religious worship. We must <hi type="italic">worship God in spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.24">John iv. 24</reference>. The work of religion is to no purpose any further than the heart is employed in it. <hi type="italic">Whatsoever we do, we must do it heartily as unto the Lord;</hi> and we must worship God in the strength and grace of the Divine Spirit, which is so peculiar to the gospel state, which is the <hi type="italic">ministration of the spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.8">2 Cor. iii. 8</reference>. 2. They <hi type="italic">rejoice in Christ Jesus,</hi> and not in the peculiar privileges of the Jewish church, or what answers to them in the Christian church—mere outward enjoyments and performances. They rejoice in their relation to Christ and interest in him. God made it the duty of the Israelites to rejoice before him in the courts of his house; but now that the substance has come the shadows are done away, and we are to rejoice in Christ Jesus only. 3. They have no <hi type="italic">confidence in the flesh,</hi> in those carnal ordinances and outward performances. We must be taken off from trusting in our own bottom, that we may build only on Jesus Christ, the everlasting foundation. Our confidence, as well as our joy, is proper to him.
entries.e96910f1cb3ff81060bab868c8e3a2ce67dcb079: <div eID="gen31974" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">False Confidence Renounced. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31975" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Though I might also have confidence in the flesh. If any other man thinketh that he hath whereof he might trust in the flesh, I more: <hi type="super">5</hi> Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, <hi type="italic">of</hi> the tribe of Benjamin, a hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee; <hi type="super">6</hi> Concerning zeal, persecuting the church; touching the righteousness which is in the law, blameless. <hi type="super">7</hi> But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. <hi type="super">8</hi> Yea doubtless, and I count all things <hi type="italic">but</hi> loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them <hi type="italic">but</hi> dung, that I may win Christ, <div eID="gen31975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31976" type="x-p"/> The apostle here proposes himself for an example of trusting in Christ only, and not in his privileges as an Israelite. <div eID="gen31976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31977" type="x-p"/> I. He shows what he had to boast of as a Jew and a Pharisee. Let none think that the apostle despised these things (as men commonly do) because he had them not himself to glory in. No, if he would have gloried and trusted in the flesh, he had as much cause to do so as any man: <hi type="italic">If any other man thinketh that he hath whereof to trust in the flesh, I more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.4">v. 4</reference>. He had as much to boast of as any Jew of them all. 1. His birth-right privileges. He was not a proselyte, but a native Israelite: <hi type="italic">of the stock of Israel.</hi> And he was <hi type="italic">of the tribe of Benjamin,</hi> in which tribe the temple stood, and which adhered to Judah when all the other tribes revolted. Benjamin was the father's darling, and this was a favourite tribe. <hi type="italic">A Hebrew of the Hebrews,</hi> an Israelite on both sides, by father and mother, and from one generation to another; none of his ancestors had matched with Gentiles. 2. He could boast of his relations to the church and the covenant, for he was <hi type="italic">circumcised the eighth day;</hi> he had the token of God's covenant in his flesh, and was circumcised the very day which God had appointed. 3. For learning, he was a Pharisee, brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, an eminent doctor of the law: and was a scholar learned in all the learning of the Jews, taught according to the perfect manner of the laws of the fathers, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.3">Acts xxii. 3</reference>. He was a <hi type="italic">Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.23.6">Acts xxiii. 6</reference>), and <hi type="italic">after the most strict sect of his religion lived a Pharisee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.5">Acts xxvi. 5</reference>. 4. He had a blameless conversation: <hi type="italic">Toughing the righteousness which is of the law, blameless:</hi> as far as the Pharisees' exposition of the law went, and as to the mere letter of the law and outward observance of it, he could acquit himself from the breach of it and could not be accused by any. 5. He had been an active man for his religion. As he made a strict profession of it, under the title and character of a Pharisee, so he persecuted those whom he looked upon as enemies to it. <hi type="italic">Concerning zeal, persecuting the church.</hi> 6. He showed that he was in good earnest, though he had a zeal without knowledge to direct and govern the exercise of it: <hi type="italic">I was zealous towards God, as you all are this day, and I persecuted this way unto the death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.22.3-Acts.22.4">Acts xxii. 3, 4</reference>. All this was enough to have made a proud Jew confident, and was stock sufficient to set up with for his justification. But, <div eID="gen31977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31978" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle tells us here how little account he made of these, in comparison of his interest in Christ and his expectations from him: <hi type="italic">But what things were gain to me those have I counted loss for Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.7">v. 7</reference>); that is, those things which he had counted gain while he was a Pharisee, and which he had before reckoned up, <hi type="italic">these he counted loss for Christ.</hi> "I should have reckoned myself an unspeakable loser of, to adhere to them, I had lost my interest in Jesus Christ." He counted them loss; not only insufficient to enrich him, but what would certainly impoverish and ruin him, if he trusted to them, in opposition to Christ. Observe, The apostle did not persuade them to do any thing but what he had himself did, to quit any thing but what he had himself quitted, nor venture on any bottom but what he himself had ventured his immortal soul upon.—<hi type="italic">Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.8">v. 8</reference>. Here the apostle explains himself. 1. He tells us what it was that he was ambitious of and reached after: it was the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord, a believing experimental acquaintance with Christ as Lord; not a merely notional and speculative, but a practical and efficacious knowledge of him. So knowledge is sometimes put for faith: <hi type="italic">By his knowledge,</hi> or the knowledge of him, <hi type="italic">shall my righteous servant justify many,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>. And it is the excellency of knowledge. There is an abundant and transcendent excellency in the doctrine of Christ, or the Christian religion above all the knowledge of nature, and improvements of human wisdom; for it is suited to the case of fallen sinners, and furnishes them with all they need and all they can desire and hope for, with all saving wisdom and saving grace. 2. He shows how he had quitted his privileges as a Jew and a Pharisee: <hi type="italic">Yea doubtless;</hi> his expression rises with a holy triumph and elevation, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">alla men oun ge kai.</hi></hi> There are five particles in the original: <hi type="italic">But indeed even also do I count all things but loss.</hi> He had spoken before of <hi type="italic">those things,</hi> his Jewish privileges: here he speaks of <hi type="italic">all things,</hi> all worldly enjoyments and mere outward privileges whatsoever, things of a like kind or any other kind which could stand in competition with Christ for the throne in his heart, or pretend to merit and desert. There he had said that he did count them but loss; but it might be asked, "Did he continue still in the same mind, did he not repent his renouncing them?" No, now he speaks in the present tense: <hi type="italic">Yea doubtless, I do count them but loss.</hi> But it may be said, "It is easy to say so; but what would he do when he came to the trial?" Why he tells us that he had himself practised according to this estimate of the case: <hi type="italic">For whom I have suffered the loss of all things.</hi> He had quitted all his honours and advantages, as a Jew and a Pharisee, and submitted to all the disgrace and suffering which attended the profession and preaching of the gospel. When he embarked in the bottom of the Christian religion, he ventured all in it, and suffered the loss of all for the privileges of a Christian. Nay, he not only counted them loss, but dung, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">skybala</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">offals</hi> thrown to dogs; they are not only less valuable than Christ, but in the highest degree contemptible, when they come in competition with him. Note, The New Testament never speaks of saving grace in any terms of diminution, but on the contrary represents it as the fruits of the divine Spirit and the image of God in the soul of man; as a divine nature, and the seed of God: and faith is called precious faith; and meekness is in the <hi type="italic">sight of God of great price,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">1 Pet. iii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.1">2 Pet. i. 1</reference>, &c.
entries.68ebcf0135e6f6ae5ac9c4f1a37615dcb88adab9: <div eID="gen31978" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Concern, Hope, and Aim. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31979" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith: <hi type="super">10</hi> That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death; <hi type="super">11</hi> If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead. <hi type="super">12</hi> Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">13</hi> Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but <hi type="italic">this</hi> one thing <hi type="italic">I do,</hi> forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, <hi type="super">14</hi> I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen31979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31980" type="x-p"/> We now heard what the apostle renounced; let us now see what he laid hold on, and resolved to cleave to, namely, Christ and heaven. He had his heart on these two great peculiarities of the Christian religion. <div eID="gen31980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31981" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle had his heart upon Christ as his righteousness. This is illustrated in several instances. 1. He desired to win Christ; and an unspeakable gainer he would reckon himself if he had but an interest in Christ and his righteousness, and if Christ became his Lord and his Saviour: <hi type="italic">That I may win him;</hi> as the runner wins the prize, as the sailor makes the port he is bound for. The expression intimates that we have need to strive for him and after him, and that all is little enough to win him. 2. That he <hi type="italic">might be found in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.9">v. 9</reference>), as the manslayer was found in the city of refuge, where he was safe from the avenger of blood, <reference osisRef="Num.35.25">Num. xxxv. 25</reference>. Or it alludes to a judicial appearance; so we are to be found of our Judge in peace, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">2 Pet. iii. 14</reference>. We are undone without a righteousness wherein to appear before God, for we are guilty. There is a righteousness provided for us in Jesus Christ, and it is a complete and perfect righteousness. None can have interest or benefit by it but those who come off from confidence in themselves, and are brought heartily to believe in him. "<hi type="italic">Not having my own righteousness, which is of the law;</hi> not thinking that my outward observances and good deeds are able to atone for my bad ones, or that by setting the one over against the other I can come to balance accounts with God. No, the righteousness which I depend upon is that <hi type="italic">which is through the faith of Christ,</hi> not a legal, but evangelical righteousness: <hi type="italic">The righteousness which is of God by faith,</hi> ordained and appointed of God." The Lord Jesus Christ is the Lord our righteousness, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Isa. xlv. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer. xxiii. 6</reference>. Had he not been God, he could not have been our righteousness; the transcendent excellence of the divine nature put such a value upon, and such a virtue into, his sufferings, that they became sufficient to satisfy for the sins of the world, and to bring in a righteousness which will be effectual to all that believe. Faith is the ordained means of actual interest and saving benefit in all the purchase of his blood. It is <hi type="italic">by faith in his blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Rom. iii. 25</reference>. 3. That he might know Christ (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings.</hi> Faith is called knowledge, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>. Knowing him here is believing in him: it is an experimental knowledge of the <hi type="italic">power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings,</hi> or feeling the transforming efficacy and virtue of them. Observe, The apostle was as ambitious of being sanctified as he was of being justified. He was as desirous to know the power of Christ's death and resurrection killing sin in him, and raising him up to newness of life, as he was to receive the benefit of Christ's death and resurrection in his justification. 4. That he might be conformable unto him, and this also is meant of his sanctification. We are then made conformable to his death when we die to sin, as Christ died for sin, when we are crucified with Christ, the flesh and affections of it mortified, and the <hi type="italic">world is crucified to us,</hi> and <hi type="italic">we to the world, by virtue of the cross of Christ.</hi> This is our conformity to his death. <div eID="gen31981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31982" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle had his heart upon heaven as his happiness: <hi type="italic">If by any means I might attain to the resurrection of the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.11">v. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen31982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31983" type="x-p"/> 1. The happiness of heaven is here called the resurrection of the dead, because, though the souls of the faithful, when they depart, are immediately with Christ, yet their happiness will not be complete till the general resurrection of the dead at the last day, when soul and body shall be glorified together. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Anastasis</hi></hi> sometimes signifies the future state. This the apostle had his eye upon; this he would attain. There will be a resurrection of the unjust, who shall arise to <hi type="italic">shame and everlasting contempt;</hi> and our care must be to escape that: but the joyful and glorious resurrection of saints is called <hi type="italic">the resurrection,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kat exochen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">by eminence,</hi> because it is in virtue of Christ's resurrection, as their head and first-fruits; whereas the wicked shall rise only by the power of Christ, as their judge. To the saints it will be indeed a resurrection, a return to bliss, and life, and glory; while the resurrection of the wicked is a rising from the grave, but a return to a second death. It is called the <hi type="italic">resurrection of the just,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">resurrection of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.29">John v. 29</reference>), and they are <hi type="italic">counted worthy to obtain that world and the resurrection from the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.20.35">Luke xx. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen31983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31984" type="x-p"/> 2. This joyful resurrection the apostle pressed towards. He was willing to do any thing, or suffer any thing, that he might attain that resurrection. The hope and prospect of it carried him with so much courage and constancy through all the difficulties he met with in his work. He speaks as if they were in danger of missing it, and coming short of it. A holy fear of coming short is an excellent means of perseverance. Observe, His care to be found in Christ was in order to his attaining the resurrection of the dead. Paul himself did not hope to attain it through his own merit and righteousness, but through the merit and righteousness of Jesus Christ. "Let me be found in Christ, that I may attain the resurrection of the dead, be found a believer in him, and interested in him by faith," Observe, <div eID="gen31984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31985" type="x-p"/> (1.) He looks upon himself to be in a state of imperfection and trial: <hi type="italic">Not as though I had already attained, or were already perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.12">v. 12</reference>. Observe, The best men in the world will readily own their imperfection in the present state. We have not yet attained, are not already perfect; there is still much wanting in all our duties, and graces, and comforts. If Paul had not attained to perfection (who had reached to so high a pitch of holiness), much less have we. Again, <hi type="italic">Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou logizomai.</hi></hi> "I make this judgment of the case; I thus reason with myself." Observe, Those who think they have grace enough give proof that they have little enough, or rather that they have none at all; because, wherever there is true grace, there is a desire of more grace, and a pressing towards the perfection of grace. <div eID="gen31985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31986" type="x-p"/> (2.) What the apostle's actings were under this conviction. Considering that he had not already attained, and had not apprehended, he pressed forward: "<hi type="italic">I follow after</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dioko</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I pursue</hi> with vigour, as one following after the game. I endeavour to get more grace and do more good, and never think I have done enough: <hi type="italic">If that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.</hi>" Observe, [1.] Whence our grace comes—from our being apprehended of Christ Jesus. It is not our laying hold of Christ first, but his laying hold of us, which is our happiness and salvation. <hi type="italic">We love him because he first loved us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.19">1 John iv. 19</reference>. Not our keeping hold of Christ, but his keeping hold of us, is our safety. We are <hi type="italic">kept by his mighty power through faith unto salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1 Pet. i. 5</reference>. Observe, [2.] What the happiness of heaven is: it is <hi type="italic">to apprehend that for which we are apprehended of Christ.</hi> When Christ laid hold of us, it was to bring us to heaven; and to apprehend that for which he apprehended us is to attain the perfection of our bliss. He adds further (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">This one thing I do</hi> (this was his great care and concern), <hi type="italic">forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth to those things which are before.</hi> There is a sinful forgetting of past sins and past mercies, which ought to be remembered for the exercise of constant repentance and thankfulness to God. But Paul forgot the things which were behind so as not to be content with present measures of grace: he was still for having more and more. So he <hi type="italic">reaches forth,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epekteinomenos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">stretched</hi> himself forward, bearing towards his point: it is expressive of a vehement concern. <div eID="gen31986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31987" type="x-p"/> (3.) The apostle's aim in these actings: <hi type="italic">I press towards the mark, for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.14">v. 14</reference>. He pressed towards the mark. As he who runs a race never takes up short of the end, but is still making forwards as fast as he can, so those who have heaven in their eye must still be pressing forward to it in holy desires and hopes, and constant endeavours and preparations. The fitter we grow for heaven the faster we must press towards it. Heaven is called here the mark, because it is that which every good Christian has in his eye; as the archer has his eye fixed upon the mark he designs to hit. <hi type="italic">For the prize of the high calling.</hi> Observe, A Christian's calling is a high calling: it is from heaven, as its original; and it is to heaven in its tendency. Heaven is the <hi type="italic">prize of the high calling;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">to brabeion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the prize</hi> we fight for, and run for, and wrestle for, what we aim at in all we do, and what will reward all our pains. It is of great use in the Christian course to keep our eye upon heaven. This is proper to give us measures in all our service, and to quicken us every step we take; and it is of God, from whom we are to expect it. <hi type="italic">Eternal life is the gift of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.23">Rom. vi. 23</reference>), but it is in Christ Jesus; through his hand it must come to us, as it is procured for us by him. There is no getting to heaven as our home but by Christ as our way.
entries.5b6f7ca720f7782110c75d6a6cfae47cd893af39: <div eID="gen31987" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Warnings and Exhortations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31988" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you. <hi type="super">16</hi> Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing. <div eID="gen31988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31989" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having proposed himself as an example, urges the Philippians to follow it. Let the same mind be in us which was in blessed Paul. We see here how he was minded; let us be like-minded, and set our hearts upon Christ and heaven, as he did. 1. He shows that this was the thing wherein all good Christians were agreed, to make Christ all in all, and set their hearts upon another world. This is that whereto we have all attained. However good Christians may differ in their sentiments about other things, this is what they are agreed in, that Christ is a Christian's all, that to win Christ and to be found in him involve our happiness both here and hereafter. And therefore let us walk by the same rule, and mind the same thing. Having made Christ our all, <hi type="italic">to us to live must be Christ.</hi> Let us agree to press towards the mark, and make heaven our end. 2. That this is a good reason why Christians who differ in smaller matters should yet bear with one another, because they are agreed in the main matter: "<hi type="italic">If in any thing you be otherwise minded</hi>—if you differ from one another, and are not of the same judgment as to meats and days, and other matters of the Jewish law—yet you must not judge one another, while you all meet now in Christ as your centre, and hope to meet shortly in heaven as your home. As for other matters of difference, lay no great stress upon them, <hi type="italic">God shall reveal even this unto you.</hi> Whatever it is wherein you differ, you must wait till God give you a better understanding, which he will do in his due time. In the mean time, <hi type="italic">as far as you have attained,</hi> you must go together in the ways of God, join together in all the great things in which you are agreed, and wait for further light in the minor things wherein you differ."
entries.582d0a74cac6e226854eab12d30ca51463d06d69: <div eID="gen31989" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle Urges His Own Example. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen31990" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Brethren, be followers together of me, and mark them which walk so as ye have us for an ensample. 18 (For many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, <hi type="italic">that they are</hi> the enemies of the cross of Christ: <hi type="super">19</hi> Whose end <hi type="italic">is</hi> destruction, whose God <hi type="italic">is their</hi> belly, and <hi type="italic">whose</hi> glory <hi type="italic">is</hi> in their shame, who mind earthly things.) <hi type="super">20</hi> For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ: <hi type="super">21</hi> Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself. <div eID="gen31990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31991" type="x-p"/> He closes the chapter with warnings and exhortations. <div eID="gen31991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31992" type="x-p"/> I. He warns them against following the examples of seducers and evil teachers (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.18-Phil.3.19">v. 18, 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen31992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31993" type="x-p"/> 1. There are many called by Christ's name who are enemies to Christ's cross, and the design and intention of it. Their walk is a surer evidence what they are than their profession. By <hi type="italic">their fruits you shall know them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.20">Matt. vii. 20</reference>. The apostle warns people against such, (1.) Very frequently: <hi type="italic">I have told you often.</hi> We so little heed the warnings given us that we have need to have them repeated. <hi type="italic">To write the same things is safe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">v. 1</reference>. (2.) Feelingly and affectionately: <hi type="italic">I now tell you weeping.</hi> Paul was upon proper occasions a weeping preacher, as Jeremiah was a weeping prophet. Observe, An old sermon may be preached with new affections; what we say often we may say again, if we say it affectionately, and are ourselves under the power of it. <div eID="gen31993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31994" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives us the characters of those who were the enemies of the cross of Christ. (1.) Whose God is their belly. They minded nothing but their sensual appetites. A wretched idol it is, and a scandal for any, but especially for Christians, to sacrifice the favour of God, the peace of their conscience, and their eternal happiness to it. Gluttons and drunkards make a god of their belly, and all their care is to please it and make provision for it. The same observance which good people give to God epicures give to their appetites. Of such he says, <hi type="italic">They serve not the Lord Jesus Christ, but their own bellies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Rom. xvi. 18</reference>. (2.) They glory in their shame. They not only sinned, but boasted of it and gloried in that of which they ought to have been ashamed. Sin is the sinner's shame, especially when it is gloried in. "They value themselves for what is their blemish and reproach." (3.) They mind earthly things. Christ came by his cross to <hi type="italic">crucify the world to us and us to the world;</hi> and those who mind earthly things act directly contrary to the cross of Christ, and this great design of it. They relish earthly things, and have no relish of the things which are spiritual and heavenly. They set their hearts and affections on earthly things; they love them, and even dote upon them, and have a confidence and complacency in them. He gives them this character, to show how absurd it would be for Christians to follow the example of such or be led away by them; and, to deter us all from so doing, he reads their doom. (4.) Whose end is destruction. Their way seems pleasant, but death and hell are at the end of it. <hi type="italic">What fruit had you then in those things whereof you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Rom. vi. 21</reference>. It is dangerous following them, though it is going down the stream; for, if we choose their way, we have reason to fear their end. Perhaps he alludes to the total destruction of the Jewish nation. <div eID="gen31994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31995" type="x-p"/> II. He proposes himself and his brethren for an example, in opposition to these evil examples: <hi type="italic">Brethren, be followers together of me, and mark those who walk as you have us for an example,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.17">v. 17</reference>. Mark them out for your pattern. He explains himself (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">v. 20</reference>) by their regard to Christ and heaven: <hi type="italic">For our conversation is in heaven.</hi> Observe, Good Christians, even while they are here on earth, have their conversation in heaven. Their <hi type="italic">citizenship</hi> is there, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">politeuma.</hi></hi> As if he had said, We stand related the that world, and are citizens of the New Jerusalem. This world is not our home, but that is. There our greatest privileges and concerns lie. And, because our citizenship is there, our conversation is there; being related to that world, we keep up a correspondence with it. The life of a Christian is in heaven, where his head is, and his home is, and where he hopes to be shortly; he <hi type="italic">sets his affections upon things above;</hi> and where his heart is there will his conversation be. The apostle had pressed them to follow him and other ministers of Christ: "Why," might they say, "you are a company of poor, despised, persecuted people, who make no figure, and pretend to no advantages in the world; who will follow you?" "Nay," says he, "but our conversation is in heaven. We have a near relation and a great pretension to the other world, and are not so mean and despicable as we are represented." It is good having fellowship with those who have fellowship with Christ, and conversation with those whose conversation is in heaven. <div eID="gen31995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31996" type="x-p"/> 1. Because we look for the Saviour from heaven (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> He is not here, he has ascended, he has entered within the veil for us; and we expect his second coming thence, to gather in all the citizens of that New Jerusalem to himself. <div eID="gen31996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31997" type="x-p"/> 2. Because at the second coming of Christ we expect to be happy and glorified there. There is good reason to have our conversation in heaven, not only because Christ is now there, but because we hope to be there shortly: <hi type="italic">Who shall change our vile bodies, that they may be fashioned like unto his glorious body,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">v. 21</reference>. There is a glory reserved for the bodies of the saints, which they will be instated in at the resurrection. The body is now at the best a <hi type="italic">vile body,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">to soma tes tapeinoseos hemon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the body of our humiliation:</hi> it has its rise and origin from the earth, it is supported out of the earth, and is subject to many diseases and to death at last. Besides, it is often the occasion and instrument of much sin, which is called the <hi type="italic">body of this death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Rom. vii. 24</reference>. Or it may be understood of its vileness when it lies in the grave; at the resurrection it will be found a vile body, resolved into rottenness and dust; the <hi type="italic">dust will return to the earth as it was,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.7">Eccl. xii. 7</reference>. But it will be made a glorious body; and not only raised again to life, but raised to great advantage. Observe, (1.) The sample of this change, and that is, the glorious body of Christ; when he was transfigured upon the mount, <hi type="italic">his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.17.2">Matt. xvii. 2</reference>. He went to heaven clothed with a body, that he might take possession of the inheritance in our nature, and be not only the <hi type="italic">first-born from the dead,</hi> but the <hi type="italic">first-born</hi> of the <hi type="italic">children of the resurrection.</hi> We shall be <hi type="italic">conformed to the image of his Son, that he may be the first-born among many brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Rom. viii. 29</reference>. (2.) The power by which this change will be wrought: <hi type="italic">According to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.</hi> There is an efficacy of power, an <hi type="italic">exceeding greatness of power,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">working of mighty power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Eph. i. 19</reference>. It is matter of comfort to us that he can subdue all things to himself, and sooner or later will bring over all into his interest. And the resurrection will be wrought by this power. <hi type="italic">I will raise him up at the last day,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.44">John vi. 44</reference>. Let this confirm our faith of the resurrection, that we not only have the scriptures, which assure us it shall be, but we <hi type="italic">know the power of God,</hi> which can effect it, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.29">Matt. xxii. 29</reference>. At Christ's resurrection was a glorious instance of the divine power, and therefore <hi type="italic">he is declared to be the Son of God with power, by the resurrection from the dead</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Rom. i. 4</reference>), so will our resurrection be: and his resurrection is a standing evidence, as well as pattern, of ours. And then all the enemies of the Redeemer's kingdom will be completely conquered. Not only he <hi type="italic">who had the power of death,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">the devil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb. ii. 14</reference>), but the <hi type="italic">last enemy, shall be destroyed,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">death,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.26">1 Cor. xv. 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">shall be swallowed up in victory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.54">v. 54</reference>.  <chapter eID="Phil.3"/> <div eID="gen31997" type="x-p"/>

entries.c0bac345dba88d829c8338de7f9b495ea8a66afb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17781"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Phil.3.1-Phil.3.21">Php 3:1-21</reference>. Warning against Judaizers: He Has Greater Cause than They to Trust in Legal Righteousness, but Renounced It for Christ's Righteousness, in Which He Presses after Perfection: Warning against Carnal Persons: Contrast of the Believer's Life and Hope.</title> <div sID="gen36036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17781"/><hi type="bold">1. Finally--</hi>rather, not with the notion of time, but making a transition to another general subject, "Furthermore" [Bengel and Wahl] as in <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.1">1Th 4:1</reference>. Literally, "As to what remains," &c. It is often used at the conclusion of Epistles for "finally" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.10">Ep 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.1">2Th 3:1</reference>). But it is not restricted to this meaning, as Alford thinks, supposing that Paul used it here intending to close his Epistle, but was led by the mention of the Judaizers into a more lengthened dissertation.<div eID="gen36036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same things--</hi>concerning "rejoicing," the prevailing feature in this Epistle (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.18">Php 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.25">25</reference>; 2:17; 4:4, where, compare the "again I say," with "the same things" here).<div eID="gen36037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">In the Lord--</hi>marks the true ground of joy, in contrast with "having confidence in the flesh," or in any outward sensible matter of boasting (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Php 3:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not grievous--</hi>"not irksome."<div eID="gen36039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for you it is safe--</hi>Spiritual joy is the best safety against error (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.2">Php 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Ne 8:10</reference>, end). <div eID="gen36040" type="x-p"/>
entries.d56e8e4b31acf22c6908e354de4b827fd791456c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17782"/><div sID="gen36041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17782"/><hi type="bold">2. Beware--</hi>Greek, "Have your eye on" so as to beware of. Contrast "mark," or "observe," namely, so as to follow <reference osisRef="Phil.3.17">Php 3:17</reference>.<div eID="gen36041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dogs--</hi>Greek, "the dogs," namely, those impure persons "of whom I have told you often" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.18">Php 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">19</reference>); "the abominable" (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.8">Re 21:8</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">Re 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Mt 7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>): "dogs" in filthiness, unchastity, and snarling (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.18">De 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.6">Psa 59:6</reference>, 14, 15; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.22">2Pe 2:22</reference>): especially "enemies of the cross of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.18">Php 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.20">20</reference>). The Jews regarded the Gentiles as "dogs" (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.26">Mt 15:26</reference>); but by their own unbelief they have ceased to be the true Israel, and are become "dogs" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.56.10">Is 56:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen36042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil workers--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">2Co 11:13</reference>), "deceitful workers." Not simply "evildoers" are meant, but men who "worked," indeed, ostensibly for the Gospel, but worked for evil: "serving not our Lord, but their own belly" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Ro 16:18</reference>). Translate, "The evil workmen," that is, bad teachers (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.15">2Ti 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">concision--</hi>Circumcision had now lost its spiritual significance, and was now become to those who rested on it as any ground of justification, a senseless mutilation. Christians have the only true circumcision, namely, that of the heart; legalists have only "concision," that is, the cutting off of the flesh. To make "cuttings in the flesh" was expressly prohibited by the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.5">Le 21:5</reference>): it was a Gentile-heathenish practice (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.28">1Ki 18:28</reference>); yet this, writes Paul indignantly, is what these legalists are virtually doing in violation of the law. There is a remarkable gradation, says Birks [Horæ Apostolicæ] in Paul's language as to circumcision. In his first recorded discourse (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.39">Ac 13:39</reference>), circumcision is not named, but implied as included in the law of Moses which cannot justify. Six or seven years later, in the Epistle to Galatians (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.3">Ga 3:3</reference>), the first Epistle in which it is named, its spiritual inefficiency is maintained against those Gentiles who, beginning in the Spirit, thought to be perfected in the flesh. Later, in Epistle to Romans (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.28">Ro 2:28</reference>, 29), he goes farther, and claims the substance of it for every believer, assigning the shadow only of it to the unbelieving Jew. In Epistle to Colossians (<reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.11">3:11</reference>), still later, he expounds more fully the true circumcision as the exclusive privilege of the believer. Last of all here, the very name is denied to the legalist, and a term of reproach is substituted, "concision," or flesh-cutting. Once obligatory on all the covenant-people, then reduced to a mere national distinction, it was more and more associated in the apostle's experience with the open hostility of the Jews, and the perverse teaching of false brethren. <div eID="gen36044" type="x-p"/>
entries.a58db96e0949047edffeab3591d596457476ce7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17783"/><div sID="gen36045" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17783"/>3. "We are the (real) circumcision" (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.25-Rom.2.29">Ro 2:25-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worship God in the Spirit--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "worship by the Spirit of God"; our religious service is rendered by the Spirit (<reference osisRef="John.4.23">Joh 4:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.24">24</reference>). Legal worship was outward, and consisted in outward acts, restricted to certain times and places. Christian worship is spiritual, flowing from the inworkings of the Holy Spirit, not relating to certain isolated acts, but embracing the whole life (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>). In the former, men trusted in something human, whether descent from the theocratic nation, or the righteousness of the law, or mortification of "the flesh" ("Having confidence," or "glorying in the flesh") [Neander] (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.9">Ro 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen36046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice in Christ Jesus--</hi>"make our boast in Christ Jesus," not in the law: the ground of their boasting.<div eID="gen36047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have no confidence in the flesh--</hi>but in the Spirit. <div eID="gen36048" type="x-p"/>
entries.a668ac23587823d25d3d21f914b187dd0ce1a034: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17784"/><div sID="gen36049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17784"/>4. "Although I (emphatical) might have confidence even in the flesh." Literally, "I having," but not using, "confidence in the flesh."<div eID="gen36049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I more--</hi>have more "whereof I might have confidence in the flesh." <div eID="gen36050" type="x-p"/>
entries.c82973fb0d5b0b8d75a8ec6ed74e07fe1c970dc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17785"/><div sID="gen36051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17785"/>5. In three particulars he shows how he "might have confidence in the flesh" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.4">Php 3:4</reference>): (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">1</reference>) His pure Jewish blood. (2) His legal preciseness and high status as such. (3) His zeal for the law. The Greek is literally, "Being in circumcision an eighth day person," that is, not one circumcised in later life as a proselyte, but on the eighth day after birth, as the law directed in the case of Jew-born infants.<div eID="gen36051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the tribe of Benjamin--</hi>son of Rachel, not of the maid-servant [Bengel].<div eID="gen36052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hebrew of the Hebrews--</hi>neither one or other parent being Gentile. The "Hebrew," wherever he dwelt, retained the language of his fathers. Thus Paul, though settled in Tarsus, a Greek city, calls himself a Hebrew. A "Grecian" or Hellenist, on the other hand, in the New Testament, is the term used for a "Greek-speaking" Jew [Trench].<div eID="gen36053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">touching the law--</hi>that is, as to legal status and strictness.<div eID="gen36054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a Pharisee--</hi>"of the straitest sect" (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.5">Ac 26:5</reference>). <div eID="gen36055" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f15e154a09a2d6babde8cad5976d82ee70b76e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17786"/><div sID="gen36056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17786"/><hi type="bold">6. Concerning--</hi>Translate as before and after, "As touching Zeal" (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.22.3">Ac 22:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.9">26:9</reference>).<div eID="gen36056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blameless--</hi>Greek, "having become blameless" as to ceremonial righteousness: having attained in the eyes of man blameless legal perfection. As to the holiness before God, which is the inner and truest spirit of the law, and which flows from "the righteousness of God by faith," he on the contrary declares (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.12-Phil.3.14">Php 3:12-14</reference>) that he has not attained perfection. <div eID="gen36057" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f740b4eb011c8907ed8b04f8baa27ff330b5bf7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17787"/><div sID="gen36058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17787"/><hi type="bold">7. gain--</hi>rather as Greek, "gains"; including all possible advantages of outward status, which he had heretofore enjoyed.<div eID="gen36058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I counted--</hi>Greek, "I have counted for Christ's sake loss." He no longer uses the plural as in "gains"; for he counts them all but one great "loss" (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Mt 16:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.25">Lu 9:25</reference>). <div eID="gen36059" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a8d0fe50dacf976b480e39663d5ecd42d88066c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17788"/><div sID="gen36060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17788"/><hi type="bold">8. Yea doubtless--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "doubtless" (Greek, "ge"): translate, "nay more." Not only "have I counted" those things just mentioned "loss for Christ's sake, but, moreover, I even DO count ALL things but loss," &c.<div eID="gen36060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the excellency--</hi>Greek, "On account of the surpassing excellency (the supereminence above them all) of the knowledge of Christ Jesus."<div eID="gen36061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my Lord--</hi>believing and loving appropriation of Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.1">Psa 63:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.28">Joh 20:28</reference>).<div eID="gen36062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for whom--</hi>"on account of whom."<div eID="gen36063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have suffered the loss--</hi>not merely I "counted" them "loss," but have actually lost them.<div eID="gen36064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things--</hi>The Greek has the article, referring to the preceding "all things"; "I have suffered the loss of them all."<div eID="gen36065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dung--</hi>Greek, "refuse (such as excrements, dregs, dross) cast to the dogs," as the derivation expresses. A "loss" is of something having value; but "refuse" is thrown away as not worthy of being any more touched or looked at.<div eID="gen36066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">win--</hi>Translate, to accord with the translation, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.7">Php 3:7</reference>, "gain Christ." A man cannot make other things his "gain" or chief confidence, and at the same time "gain Christ." He who loses all things, and even himself, on account of Christ, gains Christ: Christ is His, and He is Christ's (<reference osisRef="Song.2.16">So 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.3">6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.23">Lu 9:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.23">1Co 3:23</reference>). <div eID="gen36067" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c6c240776cf1233e015d4d9e886ab7397c7df78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17789"/><div sID="gen36068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17789"/><hi type="bold">9. be found in him--</hi>"be found" at His coming again, living spiritually "in Him" as the element of my life. Once lost, I have been "found," and I hope to be perfectly "found" by Him (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.8">Lu 15:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">own righteousness ... of the law--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Phil.3.6">Php 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Ro 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.5">5</reference>). "Of," that is, from.<div eID="gen36069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness ... of God by faith--</hi>Greek, "which is from God (resting) upon faith." Paul was transported from legal bondage into Christian freedom at once, and without any gradual transition. Hence, the bands of Pharisaism were loosed instantaneously; and opposition to Pharisaic Judaism took the place of opposition to the Gospel. Thus God's providence fitly prepared him for the work of overthrowing all idea of legal justification. "The righteousness of faith," in Paul's sense, is the righteousness or perfect holiness of Christ appropriated by faith, as the objective ground of confidence for the believer, and also as a new subjective principle of life. Hence it includes the essence of a new disposition, and may easily pass into the idea of sanctification, though the two ideas are originally distinct. It is not any arbitrary act of God, as if he treated as sinless a man persisting in sin, simply because he believes in Christ; but the objective on the part of God corresponds to the subjective on the part of man, namely, faith. The realization of the archetype of holiness through Christ contains the pledge that this shall be realized in all who are one with Him by faith, and are become the organs of His Spirit. Its germ is imparted to them in believing although the fruit of a life perfectly conformed to the Redeemer, can only be gradually developed in this life [Neander]. <div eID="gen36070" type="x-p"/>
entries.8884e88071d2e9b4bd3ac82c0a2cc01f15ba35e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17790"/><div sID="gen36071" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17790"/><hi type="bold">10. That I may know him--</hi>experimentally. The aim of the "righteousness" just mentioned. This verse resumes, and more fully explains, "the excellency of the knowledge of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.8">Php 3:8</reference>). To know HIM is more than merely to know a doctrine about Him. Believers are brought not only to redemption, but to the Redeemer Himself.<div eID="gen36071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the power of his resurrection--</hi>assuring believers of their justification (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Ro 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.17">1Co 15:17</reference>), and raising them up spiritually with Him, by virtue of their identification with Him in this, as in all the acts of His redeeming work for us (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.4">Ro 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>). The power of the Divine Spirit, which raised Him from literal death, is the same which raises believers from spiritual death now (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>), and shall raise their bodies from literal death hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the fellowship of his sufferings--</hi>by identification with Him in His sufferings and death, by imputation; also, in actually bearing the cross whatever is laid on us, after His example, and so "filling up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.24">Col 1:24</reference>); and in the will to bear aught for His sake (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.38">Mt 10:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.16.24">16:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11">2Ti 2:11</reference>). As He bore all our sufferings (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Is 53:4</reference>), so we participate in His.<div eID="gen36073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made conformable unto his death--</hi>"conformed to the likeness of His death," namely, by continued sufferings for His sake, and mortifying of the carnal self (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Ro 8:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.31">1Co 15:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10-2Cor.4.12">2Co 4:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>). <div eID="gen36074" type="x-p"/>
entries.c74e97206e6a2ccc59b71e8f963ad32b49647e30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17791"/><div sID="gen36075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17791"/><hi type="bold">11. If by any means--</hi>not implying uncertainty of the issue, but the earnestness of the struggle of faith (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.26">1Co 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">27</reference>), and the urgent need of jealous self-watchfulness (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.12">1Co 10:12</reference>).<div eID="gen36075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">attain unto the resurrection of the dead--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "the resurrection from (out of) the dead," namely, the first resurrection; that of believers at Christ's coming (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">1Co 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.15">1Th 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.5">Re 20:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.6">6</reference>). The Greek word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. "The power of Christ's resurrection" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>), ensures the believer's attainment of the "resurrection from the (rest of the) dead" (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">21</reference>). Compare "accounted worthy to obtain the resurrection from the dead" (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.35">Lu 20:35</reference>). "The resurrection of the just" (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.14">Lu 14:14</reference>). <div eID="gen36076" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b8c927bd89d077870a84aea5e15553edce857f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17792"/><div sID="gen36077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17792"/>12. Translate, "Not that I," &c. (I do not wish to be understood as saying that, &c.).<div eID="gen36077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">attained--</hi>"obtained," namely, a perfect knowledge of Christ, and of the power of His death, and fellowship of His sufferings, and a conformity to His death.<div eID="gen36078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">either were already perfect--</hi>"or am already perfected," that is, crowned with the garland of victory, my course completed, and perfection absolutely reached. The image is that of a race course throughout. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">1Co 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">He 12:23</reference>. See Trench [Greek Synonyms of the New Testament].<div eID="gen36079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I follow after--</hi>"I press on."<div eID="gen36080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">apprehend ... apprehended--</hi>"If so be that I may lay hold on that (namely, the prize, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.14">Php 3:14</reference>) for which also I was laid hold on by Christ" (namely, at my conversion, <reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>).<div eID="gen36081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts. Paul was close to "apprehending" the prize (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.7">2Ti 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">8</reference>). Christ the Author, is also the Finisher of His people's "race." <div eID="gen36082" type="x-p"/>
entries.b78643bd8eb906bb905da18ba5da53608c642eb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17793"/><div sID="gen36083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17793"/><hi type="bold">13. I--</hi>whatever others count as to themselves. He who counts himself perfect, must deceive himself by calling sin infirmity (<reference osisRef="1John.1.8">1Jo 1:8</reference>); at the same time, each must aim at perfection, to be a Christian at all (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.48">Mt 5:48</reference>).<div eID="gen36083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgetting those things ... behind--</hi>Looking back is sure to end in going back (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.62">Lu 9:62</reference>): So Lot's wife (<reference osisRef="Luke.17.32">Lu 17:32</reference>). If in stemming a current we cease pulling the oar against it, we are carried back. God's word to us is as it was to Israel, "Speak unto the children of Israel that they go forward" (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.15">Ex 14:15</reference>). The Bible is our landmark to show us whether we are progressing or retrograding.<div eID="gen36084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reaching forth--</hi>with hand and foot, like a runner in a race, and the body bent forward. The Christian is always humbled by the contrast between what he is and what he desires to be. The eye reaches before and draws on the hand, the hand reaches before and draws on the foot [Bengel].<div eID="gen36085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto--</hi>towards (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.1">He 6:1</reference>). <div eID="gen36086" type="x-p"/>
entries.50648878d7da7f285c867bb0ddd51d79a645a61b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17794"/><div sID="gen36087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17794"/><hi type="bold">14. high calling--</hi>literally, "the calling that is above" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Ga 4:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.1">Col 3:1</reference>): "the heavenly calling" (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.1">He 3:1</reference>). "The prize" is "the crown of righteousness" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">1Co 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>). <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Re 2:10</reference>, "crown of life." <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1Pe 5:4</reference>, "a crown of glory that fadeth not away." "The high," or "heavenly calling," is not restricted, as Alford thinks, to Paul's own calling as an apostle by the summons of God from heaven; but the common calling of all Christians to salvation in Christ, which coming from heaven invites us to heaven, whither accordingly our minds ought to be uplifted. <div eID="gen36087" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b4a18679ebe053ce70155981fe5835a12b2af7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17795"/><div sID="gen36088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17795"/><hi type="bold">15. therefore--</hi>resuming <reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Php 3:3</reference>. "As many of us then, as are perfect," that is, full grown (no longer "babes") in the Christian life (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Php 3:3</reference>, "worshipping God in the Spirit, and having no confidence in the flesh"), <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>, fully established in things of God. Here, by "perfect," he means one fully fit for running [Bengel]; knowing and complying with the laws of the course (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.5">2Ti 2:5</reference>). Though "perfect" in this sense, he was not yet "made perfect" (Greek) in the sense intended in <reference osisRef="Phil.3.12">Php 3:12</reference>, namely, "crowned with complete victory," and having attained absolute perfection.<div eID="gen36088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thus minded--</hi>having the mind which he had described, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.7-Phil.3.14">Php 3:7-14</reference>.<div eID="gen36089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">otherwise minded--</hi>having too high an opinion of yourselves as to your attainment of Christian perfection. "He who thinks that he has attained everything, hath nothing" [Chrysostom]. Probably, too, he refers to those who were tempted to think to attain to perfection by the law (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.3">Ga 3:3</reference>): who needed the warning (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Php 3:3</reference>), "Beware of the concision," though on account of their former piety, Paul hopes confidently (as in <reference osisRef="Gal.5.10">Ga 5:10</reference>) that God will reveal the path of right-mindedness to them. Paul taught externally God "reveals" the truth internally by His Spirit (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.25">Mt 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1Co 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto you--</hi>who sincerely strive to do God's will (<reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.17">Ep 1:17</reference>). <div eID="gen36091" type="x-p"/>
entries.68bf24b3ccd6d96c9ef2f69b62185f224ff62f75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17796"/><div sID="gen36092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17796"/>16. The expectation of a new revelation is not to make you less careful in walking according to whatever degree of knowledge of divine things and perfection you have already attained. God makes further revelations to those who walk up to the revelations they already have (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Ho 6:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rule, let us mind the same thing--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts. Perhaps partly inserted from <reference osisRef="Gal.6.16">Ga 6:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Phil.2.2">Php 2:2</reference>. Translate then, "Whereunto we have attained, let us walk on (a military term, march in order) in the same (the measure of knowledge already attained)." <div eID="gen36093" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0099ef0240c34d346fcef73da5a1b895ce46d2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17797"/><div sID="gen36094" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17797"/><hi type="bold">17. followers--</hi>Greek, "imitators together."<div eID="gen36094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36095" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of me--</hi>as I am an imitator of Christ (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1Co 11:1</reference>): Imitate me no farther than as I imitate Christ. Or as Bengel "My fellow imitators of God" or "Christ"; "imitators of Christ together with me" (see on <reference osisRef="Phil.2.22">Php 2:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.1">Ep 5:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mark--</hi>for imitation.<div eID="gen36096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which walk so as ye have us for an ensample--</hi>In English Version of the former clause, the translation of this clause is, "those who are walking so as ye have an example in us." But in Bengel's translation, "inasmuch as," or "since," instead of "as." <div eID="gen36097" type="x-p"/>
entries.c817ed8855403c594477cd73c1abf5b9ffa02d4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17798"/><div sID="gen36098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17798"/><hi type="bold">18. many walk--</hi>in such a manner. Follow not evildoers, because they are "many" (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.2">Ex 23:2</reference>). Their numbers are rather a presumption against their being Christ's "little flock" (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.32">Lu 12:32</reference>).<div eID="gen36098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">often--</hi>There is need of constant warning.<div eID="gen36099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weeping--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.9.2">Ro 9:2</reference>). A hard tone in speaking of the inconsistencies of professors is the very opposite of Paul's spirit, and David's (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.136">Psa 119:136</reference>), and Jeremiah's (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jr 13:17</reference>). The Lord and His apostles, at the same time, speak more strongly against empty professors (as the Pharisees), than against open scoffers.<div eID="gen36100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enemies of the cross of Christ--</hi>in their practice, not in doctrine (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.14">Ga 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.6">He 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">10:29</reference>). <div eID="gen36101" type="x-p"/>
entries.f748d0531a50a9cc03fb69afaadebbbffc94057a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17799"/><div sID="gen36102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17799"/><hi type="bold">19. destruction--</hi>everlasting at Christ's coming. <reference osisRef="Phil.1.28">Php 1:28</reference>, "perdition"; the opposite word is "Saviour" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>).<div eID="gen36102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">end--</hi>fixed doom.<div eID="gen36103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose god is their belly--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Ro 16:18</reference>); hereafter to be destroyed by God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">1Co 6:13</reference>). In contrast to our "body" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>), which our God, the Lord Jesus, shall "fashion like unto His glorious body." Their belly is now pampered, our body now wasted; then the respective states of both shall be reversed.<div eID="gen36104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory is in their shame--</hi>As "glory" is often used in the Old Testament for God (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.20">Psa 106:20</reference>), so here it answers to "whose God," in the parallel clause; and "shame" is the Old Testament term contemptuously given to an idol (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.32">Jud 6:32</reference>, Margin). <reference osisRef="Hos.4.7">Ho 4:7</reference> seems to be referred to by Paul (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.32">Ro 1:32</reference>). There seems no allusion to circumcision, as no longer glorious, but a shame to them (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.2">Php 3:2</reference>). The reference of the immediate context is to sensuality, and carnality in general.<div eID="gen36105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mind earthly things--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.8.5">Ro 8:5</reference>). In contrast to <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.2">Col 3:2</reference>. <div eID="gen36106" type="x-p"/>
entries.f635fdb6dc045833ade8a3213fbf2f402d32b3bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17800"/><div sID="gen36107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17800"/><hi type="bold">20. our conversation--</hi>rather, "our state" or "country"; our citizenship: our life as citizens. We are but pilgrims on earth; how then should we "mind earthly things?" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.9">He 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13-Heb.10.16">10, 13-16</reference>). Roman citizenship was then highly prized; how much more should the heavenly citizenship (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.28">Ac 22:28</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Lu 10:20</reference>)?<div eID="gen36107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is--</hi>Greek, "has its existence."<div eID="gen36108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in heaven--</hi>Greek, "in the heavens."<div eID="gen36109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>"We wait for (so the same Greek is translated, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.19">Ro 8:19</reference>) the Lord Jesus as a (that is, in the capacity of a) Saviour" (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>). That He is "the Lord," now exalted above every name, assures our expectation (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.9-Phil.2.11">Php 2:9-11</reference>). Our High Priest is gone up into the Holy of Holies not made with hands, there to atone for us; and as the Israelites stood outside the tabernacle, expecting Aaron's return (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.21">Lu 1:21</reference>), so must we look unto the heavens expecting Christ thence. <div eID="gen36110" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c16c64d6be30199dbce1e89ae6057f789093561: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17801"/><div sID="gen36111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17801"/>21. Greek, "Who shall transfigure the body of our humiliation (namely, in which our humiliation has place, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">2Co 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">Ep 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">2Ti 2:12</reference>), that it may be conformed unto the body of His glory (namely, in which His glory is manifested), according to the effectual working whereby," &c. Not only shall He come as our "Saviour," but also as our Glorifier.<div eID="gen36111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even--</hi>not only to make the body like His own, but "to subdue all things," even death itself, as well as Satan and sin. He gave a sample of the coming transfiguration on the mount (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.1">Mt 17:1</reference>, &c.). Not a change of identity, but of fashion or form (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1Co 15:51</reference>). Our spiritual resurrection now is the pledge of our bodily resurrection to glory hereafter (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>). As Christ's glorified body was essentially identical with His body of humiliation; so our resurrection bodies as believers, since they shall be like His, shall be identical essentially with our present bodies, and yet "spiritual bodies" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.42-1Cor.15.44">1Co 15:42-44</reference>). Our "hope" is, that Christ, by His rising from the dead, hath obtained the power, and is become the pattern, of our resurrection (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.13">Mi 2:13</reference>). <chapter eID="Phil.3"/>

entries.e7e3675ff4d057836251149885a47cf07866e69e: <div eID="gen50618" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen50619" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50620" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50620" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50619" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50621" type="x-p"/> The apostle exhorts the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.1">Phi 3:1</reference>. And to beware of false teachers, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.2">Phi 3:2</reference>. Shows that Christians are the true circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.3">Phi 3:3</reference>. And that himself had more reason to trust in the flesh than any of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.4-Phi.3.6">Phi 3:4-6</reference>. But that he counted all things loss for Christ, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.7-Phi.3.11">Phi 3:7-11</reference>. He longs after a conformity to Christ in his death, and presses onward to the attainment of his high calling, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.12-Phi.3.14">Phi 3:12-14</reference>. Exhorts them to be like-minded, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.15-Phi.3.17">Phi 3:15-17</reference>. Warns them against certain persons who were enemies to the cross of Christ, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.18">Phi 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.19">Phi 3:19</reference>. Shows the nature of their heavenly privileges, and the resurrection and glorification of the human body, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.20">Phi 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phi.3.21">Phi 3:21</reference>.
