10 That I may know him He points out the efficacy and nature of faith — that it is the knowledge of Christ, and that, too, not bare or indistinct, but in such a manner that the power of his resurrection is felt. Resurrection he employs as meaning, the completion of redemption, so that it comprehends in it at the same time the idea of death. But as it is not enough to know Christ as crucified and raised up from the dead, unless you experience, also, the fruit of this, he speaks expressly of efficacy.
“De l’efficace ou puissance;” — “Of the efficacy or power.”
Christ therefore is rightly known, when we feel how powerful his death and resurrection are, and how efficacious they are in us. Now all things are there furnished to us — expiation and destruction of sin, freedom from condemnation, satisfaction, victory over death, the attainment of righteousness, and the hope of a blessed immortality.
And the fellowship of his sufferings Having spoken of that freely-conferred righteousness, which was procured for us through the resurrection of Christ, and is obtained by us through faith, he proceeds to treat of the exercises of the pious, and that in order that it might not seem as though he introduced an inactive faith, which produces no effects in the life. He also intimates, indirectly, that these are the exercises in which the Lord would have his people employ themselves; while the false Apostles pressed forward upon them the useless elements of ceremonies. Let every one, therefore, who has become through faith a partaker of all Christ’s benefits, acknowledge that a condition is presented to him — that his whole life be conformed to his death.
There is, however, a twofold participation and fellowship in the death of Christ. The one is inward — what the Scripture is wont to term the mortification of the flesh, or the crucifixion of the old man, of which Paul treats in the sixth chapter of the Romans; the other is outward — what is termed the mortification of the outward man. It is the endurance of the Cross, of which he treats in the eighth chapter of the same Epistle, and here also, if I do not mistake. For after introducing along with this the power of his resurrection, Christ crucified is set before us, that we may follow him through tribulations and distresses; and hence the resurrection of the dead is expressly made mention of, that we may know that we must die before we live. This is a continued subject of meditation to believers so long as they sojourn in this world.
This, however, is a choice consolation, that in all our miseries we are partakers of Christ’s Cross, if we are his members; so that through afflictions the way is opened up for us to everlasting blessedness, as we read elsewhere,
If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him. (2 Timothy 2:11,)
We must all therefore be prepared for this — that our whole life shall represent nothing else than the image of death, until it produce death itself, as the life of Christ is nothing else than a prelude of death. We enjoy, however, in the mean time, this consolation — that the end is everlasting blessedness. For the death of Christ is connected with the resurrection. Hence Paul says, that he is conformed to his death, that he may attain the glory of the resurrection. The phrase, if by any means, does not indicate doubt, but expresses difficulty, with a view to stimulate our earnest endeavor
“Afin de nous resueiller et aiguiser a nous y addonner de tant plus grande affection;” — “That it may arouse and stimulate us to devote ourselves to it with so much greater zeal.”
for it is no light contest, inasmuch as we must struggle against so many and so serious hinderances.
Philippians 3:12-17
12. Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.
12. Non quod iam apprehenerim, aut iam perfectus sim; sequor autem, si ego quoque appreehendam, quemadmodum
“Comme, ou, pour laquelle cause;” —”As, or, for which cause.”
et apprehensus sum a Christo Iesu.
13. Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before,
13. Fratres, ego me ipsum nondum arbitror apprehendisse, unum autem, eq que retro sunt oblitus, ad ea quae ante sunt me extendens,
14. I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
14. Secundum scopum sequor ad palmam supernae vocataionis Dei in Christo Iesu
15. Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you.
15. Quicunque perfecti sumus, hoc sentiamus: et si quod aliter sentitis, etiam hoc vobis Deus revelabit.
16. Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing.
16. Caeterum quo perveniamus, ut idem sentiamus, eadem procedamus regula.
17. Brethren, be followers together of me, and mark them which walk so as ye have us for an ensample.
17. Simul imitatorres mei estote, fratres, et considerate eos qui sic ambulant: quemadmodum nos habetis pro exemplari.
entries.9dc31237d0e57bdcc759ba8656b8368a73fb2258: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.3.12" sID="gen126754" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12</hi> <hi type="italic">Not as though I had already apprehended</hi> Paul insists upon <hi type="italic">this, </hi>that he may convince the Philippians that he thinks of nothing but Christ — knows nothing else — desires nothing else — is occupied with no other subject of meditation. In connection with this, there is much weight in what he now adds — that he himself, while he had given up all hinderances, had nevertheless not attained <hi type="italic">that </hi>object of aim, and that, on this account, he always aimed and eagerly aspired at something further. How much more was this incumbent on the Philippians, who were still far behind him?<div eID="gen126755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126756" type="x-p"/>It is asked, however, what it is that Paul says he has not yet attained? For unquestionably, so soon as we are by faith ingrafted into the body of Christ, we have already entered the kingdom of God, and, as it is stated in <reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.6">Ephesians 2:6</reference>, we already, in hope, <hi type="italic">sit in heavenly places. </hi>I answer, that our salvation, in the mean time, is in hope, so that the inheritance indeed is secure; but we nevertheless have it not as yet in possession. At the same time, Paul here looks at something else — the advancement of faith, and of that mortification of which he had made mention. He had said that he aimed and eagerly aspired at the resurrection of the dead through fellowship in the Cross of Christ. He adds, that he has not as yet arrived at this. At what? At the attainment of having entire fellowship in Christ’s sufferings, having a full taste of the power of his resurrection, and knowing him perfectly. He teaches, therefore, by his own example, that we ought to make progress, and that the knowledge of Christ is an attainment of such difficulty, that even those who apply themselves exclusively to it, do nevertheless not attain perfection in it so long as they live. This, however, does not detract in any degree from the authority of Paul’s doctrine, inasmuch as he had acquired as much as was sufficient for discharging the office committed to him. In the mean time, it was necessary for him to make progress, that this divinely-furnished instructor of all might be trained to humility.<div eID="gen126756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126757" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">As also I have been apprehended</hi> This clause he has inserted by way of correction, that he might ascribe all his endeavors to the grace of God. It is not of much importance whether you read <hi type="italic">as, </hi>or <hi type="italic">in so far as; </hi>for the meaning in either case remains the same — that Paul was apprehended by Christ, that he might apprehend Christ; that is, that he did nothing except under Christ’s influence and guidance. I have chosen, however, the more distinct rendering, as it seemed to be optional.<div eID="gen126757" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126754" osisID="Phil.3.12" type="section"/>
entries.27ed7160a657e8da4d76aec50560a458074d6191: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.3.13" sID="gen126758" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13</hi> <hi type="italic">I reckon not myself to have as yet apprehended</hi> He does not here call in question the certainty of his salvation, as though he were still in suspense, but repeats what he had said before — that he still aimed at making farther progress, because he had not yet attained the end of his calling. He shews this immediately after, by saying that he was intent on this one thing, leaving off everything else. Now, he compares our life to a race-course, the limits of which God has marked out to us for running in. For as it would profit the runner nothing to have left the starting-point, unless he went forward to the goal, so we must also pursue the course of our calling until death, and must not cease until we have obtained what we seek. Farther, as the way is marked out to the runner, that he may not fatigue himself to no purpose by wandering in this direction or in that, so there is also a goal set before us, towards which we ought to direct our course undeviatingly; and God does not permit us to wander about heedlessly. Thirdly, as the runner requires to be free from entanglement, and not stop his course on account of any impediment, but must continue his course, surmounting every obstacle, so we must take heed that we do not apply our mind or heart to anything that may divert the attention, but must, on the contrary, make it our endeavor, that, free from every distraction, we may apply the whole bent of our mind exclusively to God’s calling. These three things Paul comprehends in one similitude. When he says that he <hi type="italic">does this one thing, </hi>and forgets all things that are behind, he intimates his assiduity, and excludes everything fitted to distract. When he says that he <hi type="italic">presses toward the mark, </hi>he intimates that he is not wandering from the way.<div eID="gen126759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126760" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Forgetting those things that are behind</hi> He alludes to runners, who do not turn their eyes aside in any direction, lest they should slacken the speed of their course, and, more especially, do not look behind to see how much ground they have gone over, but hasten forward unremittingly towards the goal, Thus Paul teaches us, that he does not think of what he has been, or of what he has done, but simply presses forward towards the appointed goal, and that, too, with such ardor, that he runs forward to it, as it were, with outstretched arms. For a metaphor of this nature is implied in the participle which he employs. <note n="191"> <div sID="gen126761" type="x-p"/> The participle referred to is <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπεκτεινόμενος</foreign>, which, as is remarked by Dr. Bloomfield, “is highly appropriate to the <hi type="italic">racer, </hi>whether on foot, or on horseback, or in the chariot; since the racer <hi type="italic">stretches his head and hands forward </hi>in anxiety to reach the goal.” — Ed.<div eID="gen126761" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen126760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126762" type="x-p"/>Should any one remark, by way of objection, that the remembrance of our past life is of use for stirring us up, both because the favors that have been already conferred upon us give us encouragement to entertain hope, and because we are admonished by our sins to amend our course of life, I answer, that thoughts of this nature do not turn away our view from what is before us to what is behind, but rather help our vision, so that we discern more distinctly the goal. Paul, however, condemns here such looking back, as either destroys or impairs alacrity. Thus, for example, should any one persuade himself that he has made sufficiently great progress, reckoning that he has done enough, he will become indolent, and feel inclined to <hi type="italic">deliver up the lamp</hi> <note n="192"> <div sID="gen126763" type="x-p"/> A proverbial expression, founded on the circumstance that in certain games at Athens the runners had to carry a lamp, or burning torch, in such a way that it should not go out, and, on any one of the competitors giving up the contest, he <hi type="italic">delivered up the lamp, </hi>or torch, to his successor, See Auct. ad Herenn. 1. 4, c. 46; Lucret. I. 2, 5:77 — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen126763" type="x-p"/> </note> to others; or, if any one looks back with a feeling of regret for the situation that he has abandoned, he cannot apply the whole bent of his mind to what he is engaged in. Such was the nature of the thoughts from which Paul’s mind required to be turned away, if he would in good earnest follow out Christ’s calling. As, however, there has been mention made here of endeavor, aim, course, perseverance, lest any one should imagine that salvation consists in these things, or should even ascribe to human industry what comes from another quarter, with the view of pointing out the cause of all these things, he adds — <hi type="italic">in Christ Jesus</hi><div eID="gen126762" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126758" osisID="Phil.3.13" type="section"/>
entries.5e6b5dc06a586182e47ae3ecb24c097be7fdbd8e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.3.15" sID="gen126764" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15</hi> <hi type="italic">As many as are perfect</hi> Lest any one should understand this as spoken of the generality of mankind, as though he were explaining the simple elements to those that are mere children in Christ, he declares that it is a rule which all that are perfect ought to follow. Now, the rule is this — that we must renounce confidence in all things, that we may glory in Christ’s righteousness alone, and preferring it to everything else, aspire after a participation in his sufferings, which may be the means of conducting us to a blessed resurrection. Where now will be that state of perfection which monks dream of — where the confused medley of such contrivances — where, in short, the whole system of Popery, which is nothing else than an imaginary perfection, that has nothing in common with this rule of Paul? Undoubtedly, whoever will understand this single term, will clearly perceive that everything that is taught in the Papacy, as to the attainment of righteousness and salvation, is nauseous dung.<div eID="gen126765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126766" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">If in anything otherwise</hi> By the same means he both humbles them, and inspires them with good hope, for he admonishes them not to be elated in their ignorance, and at the same time he bids them be of good courage, when he says that we must wait for the revelation of God. For we know how great an obstacle to truth obstinacy is. This, therefore, is the best preparation for docility — when we do not take pleasure in error. Paul, accordingly, teaches indirectly, that we must make way for the revelation of God, if we have not yet attained what we seek. Farther, when he teaches that we must advance by degrees, he encourages them not to draw back in the middle of the course. At the same time, he maintains beyond all controversy what he has previously taught, when he teaches that others who differ from him will have a revelation given to them of what they do not as yet know. For it is as though he had said, — “The Lord will one day shew you that the very thing which I have stated is a perfect rule of true knowledge and of right living.” No one could speak in this manner, if he were not fully assured of the reasonableness and accuracy of his doctrine. Let us in the mean time learn also from this passage, that we must bear for a time with ignorance in our weak brethren, and forgive them, if it is not given them immediately to be altogether of one mind with us. Paul felt assured as to his doctrine, and yet he allows those who could not as yet receive it time to make progress, and he does not cease on that account to regard them as brethren, only he cautions them against flattering themselves in their ignorance. The rendering of the Latin copies <note n="193"> <div sID="gen126767" type="x-p"/> The rendering of the Vulgate <hi type="italic">(</hi><foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">revelavit</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">) </hi>is followed in the Rheims version — (1582) — hath <hi type="italic">revealed.</hi>—<hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen126767" type="x-p"/> </note> in the preterite, <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">revelavit</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>(he <hi type="italic">has revealed,) </hi>I have no hesitation in rejecting as unsuitable and inappropriate.<div eID="gen126766" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126764" osisID="Phil.3.15" type="section"/>
entries.bf797a07deef01149ff3df917beef6d27aaef14c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.3.16" sID="gen126768" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16</hi> <hi type="italic">Nevertheless, so far as we have attained</hi> Even the Greek manuscripts themselves differ as to the dividing of the clauses, for in some of them there are two complete sentences. If any one, however, prefer to divide the verse, the meaning will be as Erasmus has rendered it. <note n="194"> <div sID="gen126770" type="x-p"/> The rendering of Erasmus is as follows:— “<foreign xml:lang="la">Eadem incedamus regula,<hi type="italic"> ut simus concordes</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">;</hi>” — “Let us walk by the same rule, <hi type="italic">that we may be of the same mind.” </hi>The words inserted in the common text <foreign xml:lang="el">κανόνι τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν</foreign><hi type="italic"> rule</hi>—<hi type="italic">mind the same thing,) </hi>are omitted, as is noticed by Granville Penn, in the <hi type="italic">Vat. </hi>and <hi type="italic">Alex. </hi>MSS., the <hi type="italic">Copt. </hi>and <hi type="italic">Ethiop. </hi>versions, and by Hilary and Augustine. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen126770" type="x-p"/> </note> For my part, I rather prefer a different reading, implying that Paul exhorts the Philipplans to imitate him, that they may at last reach the same goal, so as to <hi type="italic">think the same thing, </hi>and <hi type="italic">walk by the same rule</hi> For where sincere affection exists, such as reigned in Paul, the way is easy to a holy and pious concord, As, therefore, they had not yet learned what true perfection was, in order that they might attain it he wishes them to be imitators of him; that is, to seek God with a <hi type="italic">pure conscience, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:2Tim.1.3">2 Timothy 1:3</reference>,) to arrogate nothing to themselves, and calmly to subject their understandings to Christ. For in the imitating of Paul all these excellences are included — pure zeal, fear of the Lord, modesty, self-renunciation, docility, love, and desire of concord. He bids them, however, be at one and the same time imitators of him; that is, all with one consent, and with one mind.<div eID="gen126769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126771" type="x-p"/>Observe, that the goal of perfection to which he invites the Philippians, by his example, is, that they <hi type="italic">think the same thing, </hi>and <hi type="italic">walk by the same rule</hi> He has, however, assigned the first place to the doctrine in which they ought to harmonize, and the rule to which they should conform themselves.<div eID="gen126771" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126768" osisID="Phil.3.16" type="section"/>
entries.a74404de49eb9f952753f04fcbd64fbf23f0e752:
17 Mark them By this expression he means, that it is all one to him what persons they single out for themselves for imitation, provided they conform themselves to that purity of which he was a pattern. By this means all suspicion of ambition is taken away, for the man that is devoted to his own interests wishes to have no rival. At the same time he warns them that all are not to be imitated indiscriminately, as he afterwards explains more fully.
Philippians 3:18-21
18. (For many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ:
18. Multi enim ambulant (quos saepe dicebam vobis, ac nunc etiam flens dico, inimicos esse crucis Christi:
19. Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)
19. Quorum finis perditio, quorum deus venter est, et gloria in confusione ipsorum terrena cogitantes.)
20. For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
20. Nostra qutem conversatio in coelis est, e quibus etiam salvatorem respectamus, Dominum Iesum Christum.
21. Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.

18 For many walk The simple statement, in my opinion, is this — Many walk who mind earthly things, meaning by this, that there are many who creep upon the ground
“Qui ont leurs affections enracines en la terre;” — “Who have their affections rooted in the earth.”
, not feeling the power of God’s kingdom. He mentions, however, in connection with this, the marks by which such persons may be distinguished. These we will examine, each in its order. By earthly things some understand ceremonies, and the outward elements of the world, which cause true piety to be forgotten, I prefer, however, to view the term as referring to carnal affection, as meaning that those who are not regenerated by the Spirit of God think of nothing but the world. This will appear more distinctly from what follows; for he holds them up to odium on this ground — that, being desirous exclusively of their own honor, ease, and gain, they had no regard to the edification of the Church.
Of whom I have told you often He shews that it is not without good reason that he has often warned the Philippians, inasmuch as he now endeavors to remind them by letter of the same things as he had formerly spoken of to them when present with them. His tears, also, are an evidence that he is not influenced by envy or hatred of men, nor by any disposition to revile, nor by insolence of temper, but by pious zeal, inasmuch as he sees that the Church is miserably destroyed
“Perdue et ruinee;” — “Destroyed and ruined.”
by such pests. It becomes us, assuredly, to be affected in such a manner, that on seeing that the place of pastors is occupied by wicked and worthless persons, we shall sigh, and give evidence, at least by our tears, that we feel deeply grieved for the calamity of the Church.
It is of importance, also, to take notice of whom Paul speaks — not of open enemies, who were avowedly desirous that doctrine might be undermined — but of impostors and profligates, who trampled under foot the power of the gospel, for the sake of ambition or of their own belly. And unquestionably persons of this sort, who weaken the influence of the ministry by seeking their own interests,
“Ne regardans qu’a eux-mesmes et a leur proufit, font perdre toutela faueur et la force du ministere;” — “Looking merely to themselves and their own advantage, undermine all the influence and power of the ministry.”
sometimes do more injury than if they openly opposed Christ. We must, therefore, by no means spare them, but must point them out with the finger, as often as there is occasion. Let them complain afterwards, as much as they choose, of our severity, provided they do not allege anything against us that it is not in our power to justify from Paul’s example.
That they are the enemies of the cross of Christ. Some explain cross to mean the whole mystery of redemption, and they explain that this is said of them, because, by preaching the law, they made void the benefit of Christ’s death. Others, however, understand it as meaning, that they shunned the cross, and were not prepared to expose themselves to dangers for the sake of Christ. I understand it, however, in a more general way, as meaning that, while they pretended to be friends, they were, nevertheless, the worst enemies of the gospel. For it is no unusual thing for Paul to employ the term cross to mean the entire preaching of the gospel. For as he says elsewhere,
If any man is in Christ, let him be a new creature. (2 Corinthians 5:17.)
Such is Calvin’s rendering of the passage referred to. See Calvin on the Corinthians, vol. 2, pp. 229, 233.—Ed.
entries.f3229572f14c2e97e23dfc02e7c64251555c2d62: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.3.19" sID="gen126795" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19</hi> <hi type="italic">Whose end is destruction</hi> He adds this in order that the Philippians, appalled by the danger, may be so much the more carefully on their guard, that they may not involve themselves in the ruin of those persons. As, however, profligates of this description, by means of show and various artifices, frequently dazzle the eyes of the simple for a time, in such a manner that they are preferred even to the most eminent servants of Christ, the Apostle declares, with great confidence <note n="199"> <div sID="gen126797" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">“</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Hardiment </hi>et d’vne grande asseurance</foreign>;” — “<hi type="italic">Boldly</hi>, and with great confidence.”<div eID="gen126797" type="x-p"/> </note> , that the glory with which they are now puffed up will be exchanged for ignominy.<div eID="gen126796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126798" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Whose god is the belly</hi> As they pressed the observance of circumcision and other ceremonies, he says that they did not do so from zeal for the law, but with a view to the favor of men, and that they might live peacefully and free from annoyance. For they saw that the Jews burned with a fierce rage against Paul, and those like him, and that Christ could not be proclaimed by them in purity with any other result, than that of arousing against themselves the same rage. Accordingly, consulting their own ease and advantage, they mixed up these corruptions with the view of mitigating the flames of others. <note n="200"> <div sID="gen126799" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour esteindre et appaiser le feu des nutres</foreign>;” — “For the sake of mitigating and allaying the fire of others.” Calvin’s meaning appears to be, that they made it their endeavor to screen themselves as far as possible from the fiery <hi type="italic">rage </hi>of those around them. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen126799" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen126798" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126795" osisID="Phil.3.19" type="section"/>
entries.6adcaeb34ea7361212a0ed71946dff6fa7df5585: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.3.20" sID="gen126800" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20</hi> <hi type="italic">But our conversation is in heaven</hi> This statement overturns all empty shows, in which pretended ministers of the gospel are accustomed to glory, and he indirectly holds up to odium all their objects of aim, <note n="201"> <div sID="gen126802" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Toutes leurs inuentions et facons de faire</foreign>;” — “All their contrivances and modes of acting.”<div eID="gen126802" type="x-p"/> </note> because, by flying about above the earth, they do not aspire towards heaven. For he teaches that nothing is to be reckoned of any value except God’s spiritual kingdom, because believers ought to lead a heavenly life in this world. <hi type="italic">“They mind earthly things: </hi>it is therefore befitting that we, whose <hi type="italic">conversation is in heaven, </hi>should be separated from them.” <note n="202"> <div sID="gen126803" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que nous soyons diuisez et separez d’auec eux</foreign>;” — “That we be divided and separated from them.”<div eID="gen126803" type="x-p"/> </note> We are, it is true, intermingled here with unbelievers and hypocrites; nay more, the chaff has more of appearance in the granary of the Lord than wheat. Farther, we are exposed to the common inconveniences of this earthly life; we require, also, meat and drink, and other necessaries, but we must, nevertheless, be conversant with heaven in mind and affection. For, on the one hand, we must pass quietly through this life, and, on the other hand, we must be dead to the world that Christ may live in us, and that we, in our turn, may live to him. This passage is a most abundant source of many exhortations, which it were easy for any one to elicit from it.<div eID="gen126801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126804" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Whence also.</hi> From the connection that we have with Christ, he proves that our citizenship <note n="203"> <div sID="gen126805" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Politiam</hi></foreign> — <hi type="italic">a </hi>term corresponding to that employed in the original,.—Ed.<div eID="gen126805" type="x-p"/> </note> is in heaven, for it is not seemly that the members should be separated from their Head. Accordingly, as Christ is in heaven, in order that we may be conjoined with him, it is necessary that we should in spirit dwell apart from this world. Besides,<div eID="gen126804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126806" type="x-p"/>where our treasure is, there is our heart also.<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.21">Matthew 6:21</reference>.)<div eID="gen126806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126807" type="x-p"/>Christ, who is our blessedness and glory, is in heaven: let our souls, therefore, dwell with him on high. On this account he expressly calIs him <hi type="italic">Savior. </hi>Whence does salvation come to us? Christ will come to us from heaven as a <hi type="italic">Savior. </hi>Hence it were unbefitting that we should be taken up with this earth <note n="204"> <div sID="gen126808" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que nous soyons occupez et enueloppez en terre</foreign>;” — “That we should be occupied and entangled with the earth.”<div eID="gen126808" type="x-p"/> </note> . This epithet, <hi type="italic">Savior, </hi>is suited to the connection of the passage; for we are said to be in heaven in respect of our minds on this account, that it is from that source alone that the hope of salvation beams forth upon us. As the coming of Christ will be terrible to the wicked, so it rather turns away their minds from heaven than draws them thither: for they know that he will come to them as a Judge, and they shun him so far as is in their power. From these words of Paul pious minds derive the sweetest consolation, as instructing them that the coming of Christ is to be desired by them, inasmuch as it will bring salvation to them. On the other hand, it is a sure token of incredulity, when persons tremble on any mention being made of it. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8">the <hi type="italic">eighth </hi>chapter of the Romans</reference>. While, however, others are transported with vain desires, Paul would have believers contented with Christ alone.<div eID="gen126807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen126809" type="x-p"/>Farther, we learn from this passage that nothing mean or earthly is to be conceived of as to Christ, inasmuch as Paul bids us look upward to heaven, that we may seek him. Now, those that reason with subtlety that Christ is not shut up or hid in some corner of heaven, with the view of proving that his body is everywhere, and fills heaven and earth, say indeed something that is true, but not the whole: for as it were rash and foolish to mount up beyond the heavens, and assign to Christ a station, or seat, or place of walking, in this or that region, so it is a foolish and destructive madness to draw him down from heaven by any carnal consideration, so as to seek him upon earth. Up, then, with our hearts <note n="205"> <div sID="gen126810" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Sursum corda</hi></foreign> Our Author most probably alludes to the circumstance, that this expression was wont to be made use of among Christians in ancient times, when the ordinance of the supper was about to be administered. See Calvin’s <hi type="italic">Institutes</hi>, vol. 3, p. 440 — Ed.<div eID="gen126810" type="x-p"/> </note> , that they may be with the Lord.<div eID="gen126809" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.3.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126800" osisID="Phil.3.20" type="section"/>

21 Who will change By this argument he stirs up the Philippians still farther to lift up their minds to heaven, and be wholly attached to Christ — because this body which we carry about with us is not an everlasting abode, but a frail tabernacle, which will in a short time be reduced to nothing. Besides, it is liable to so many miseries, and so many dishonorable infirmities, that it may justly be spoken of as vile and full of ignominy. Whence, then, is its restoration to be hoped for? From heaven, at Christ’s coming. Hence there is no part of us that ought not to aspire after heaven with undivided affection. We see, on the one hand, in life, but chiefly in death, the present meanness of our bodies; the glory which they will have, conformably to Christ’s body, is incomprehensible by us: for if the disciples could not endure the slight taste which he afforded
“De sa Gloire;” — “Of his glory.”
in his transfiguration, (Matthew 17:6,) which of us could attain its fullness? Let us for the present be contented with the evidence of our adoption, being destined to know the riches of our inheritance when we shall come to the enjoyment of them.
According to the efficacy As nothing is more difficult to believe, or more at variance with carnal perception, than the resurrection, Paul on this account places before our eyes the boundless power of God, that it may entirely remove all doubt; for distrust arises from this — that we measure the thing itself by the narrowness of our own understanding. Nor does he simply make mention of power, but also of efficacy, which is the effect, or power showing itself in action, so to speak. Now, when we bear in mind that God, who created all things out of nothing, can command the earth, and the sea, and the other elements, to render back what has been committed to them
“Qu’il leur auoit donne en garde;” — “What he had given to them to keep.”
, our minds are imrnediately roused up to a firm hope — nay, even to a spiritual contemplation of the resurrection.
But it is of importance to take notice, also, that the right and power of raising the dead, nay more, of doing everything according to his own pleasure, is assigned to the person of Christ — an encomium by which his Divine majesty is illustriously set forth. Nay, farther, we gather from this, that the world was created by him, for to subject all things to himself belongs to the Creator alone.

3. Sane rogo etiam to, germane compar, adiuva eas, quae in evangelio idem mecum certamen sustinuerunt, cum Clemente etiam, et reliquis adiutoribus meis, quorum nomina sunt in libro vitae.

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:498" />3 For we <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">In opposition to, and confutation of the <ns0:hi>Concision,</ns0:hi> he speaks of himself, and all true Believers in the fellowship of the Gospel, partakers of the same Grace and Spirit with him, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.5, 7. & 2.1. and saith We.</ns0:note> are the circumcision <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Using a Metonymie, <ns0:hi>are the Circumcision</ns0:hi> now acceptable, and not displeasing to God, <ns0:hi>i.</ns0:hi> e. we are what is really signified by it, and therefore as to the main intent of it are <ns0:hi>the</ns0:hi> Circumcised (it being usual to put <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>Circumcis'd, Act.</ns0:hi> 11.2. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.30. & 4.12. & 15.8. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.7, 8, 9, 12. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.11. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.10) he doth not mean with respect to carnal Circumcision, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> which is <ns0:hi>outward</ns0:hi> in the Flesh, but which is <ns0:hi>inward</ns0:hi> in the Spirit, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.28, 29. made without hands by the Circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cision of Christ, with whom we are buried in Baptism, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.11.12. and being Christ's are <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s spiritual Seed, and Heirs of the Promise, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.29.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 4.23.</ns0:note> which worship God in the spirit <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Who having cut off all carnal confidence of Salvation, in any external servi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces (which they of the concision contend for) and do Wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship God not with carnal, but spiritual Worship, such as now under the Gospel he doth require, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4.23, 24. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.9. from a renewed heart, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.8. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.15. yielding peculiar adoration to the Lord our God, with a sincere mind, and by the assistance of his Spirit in the exercise of Faith and Love, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.5, 6, 26, 27. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 3.16, 17. & 6.18. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.22. according to the same rule he hath prescribed, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16. with <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.1, 2. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.16. in and through Christ, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.15.</ns0:note>, and rejoice in Christ Jesus <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In whom alone (not in <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> also as false Teachers would join them) glorying we trust for accep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance with God, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.9. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.14. in communion with whom is ground of rejoicing through Christ, who is the substance or body of <ns0:hi>Mosaick</ns0:hi> shadows, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9.</ns0:note>, and have no confidence in the flesh <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">And not rest, or trust, or place our hope in any carnal or external privilege or performance, or any other besides Jesus Christ to commend us to God, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.2, 11, 12, 13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Though I might also have confidence in the flesh <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To prevent any cavil about what he said as if he did mag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifie Christ, and forbear glorying in those external privileges they did so much bear themselves upon, out of envie to them, for what they had; he here argues upon supposition (as else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where to cut off occasion from Boasters, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.12, 18, 21, 22.) that if it were lawfull, and would turn to any good ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count to confide in the flesh, he had the same ground the Impostours had, and might build up that in himself which he had destroyed in others, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.18.</ns0:note>. If any other man thinketh that he hath whereof he might trust in the flesh, I more <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Yea, and to com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pare things by a just balance, if any of those he had justly taxed, or any other that in conceit might hold his head higher in that way, he could produce not onely as much, but much more ground of trust in those external Rites, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> as he that was most excellent; onely that it was in vain, and of no value, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                  </ns0:gap> Circumcised the eighth day <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or there was, or <ns0:hi>I had the eighth day Circumcision</ns0:hi>; so it may by a usual supply of the Verb be read, (as also what follows) without a <ns0:hi>Metonymie.</ns0:hi> He begins with his birth Privilege, intimating that he was not proselyted, but Born within the pale of the Church, and dedicated to God under the seal of the Covenant at the day of God's ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointment, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 17.12.</ns0:note>, of the stock of Israel <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Not sprung from <ns0:hi>Ethnic</ns0:hi> Pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rents, not an <ns0:hi>Ishmaelite,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Edomite,</ns0:hi> but a genuine <ns0:hi>Israe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lite Rom.</ns0:hi> 11.1. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.22.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>of</ns0:hi>

                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap> the tribe of Benjamin <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Of that more honest division where the Temple stood, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 18.28. of the tribe of <ns0:hi>Benjamin</ns0:hi> the Son of beloved <ns0:hi>Rachel,</ns0:hi> and his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther's Darling, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 44.20. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 21.10. under God's special protection, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33.12. forward in the Reformation, <ns0:hi>Ezra,</ns0:hi> 1.5.</ns0:note>, an He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew of the Hebrews <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">A true descendant by <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> from <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> the Father of the faithfull, called an <ns0:hi>Hebrew (Heber</ns0:hi> joined not in building) <ns0:hi>Babel Gen.</ns0:hi> 10.21, 25. & 14.13. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 4.6. signifying that he was of the truly ancient Lineage which retained the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Tongue, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8.33, 39. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 22.2. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.12. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.22.</ns0:note>: as touching the law, a Pharisee <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">By Religion and stricter observation of the Law, according to the prescript most in vogue, of that <ns0:hi>Sect</ns0:hi> which for Learning, knowledge of the Scripture, and reputation for Holiness, was the most emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nent, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 26.5. yea, and his Father was of this Order be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />fore him, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 23.6.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Concerning zeal <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Not lukewarm, but exceeding fervent in the strictest observances of the <ns0:hi>Pharisaic</ns0:hi> Order, which was much in ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternal Devotion, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 18.12. very soli<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>itous for Proselytes, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 23.15, 25. (and his zeal had been very commendable had it been in a good matter, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.18.) that which the false Apostles contended much for.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 8.3.</ns0:note> persecuting the church <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which he shewed all manner of ways in his rage against the Church of Christ, (conceived by the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> to be opposite to the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses, Act.</ns0:hi> 9.1. & 22.3, 4. & 26.9, 10, 11, 12<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>

This external performance he found when enlightned, was far short of internal and perfect obedience, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.7. and therefore he saw it necessary to change the ground and foundation of his confidence, all that he before rested on unto Christ alone, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.11. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.17. not seeking to receive honour from Men, but that from Christ onely, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.44.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 But what things <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Having argued how he might have had as great a plea for confidence of his acceptance with God as any, if it would have held from the recited particulars, he now shews.</ns0:note> were gain to me <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">How advantagious soever they had, in the judgment of others aswell as himself, been reckoned to be, before he was effectually called.</ns0:note>, those I counted loss for Christ <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Yet, since the scales fell off his eyes that he could discern the truth, he was so far from accounting them profitable, that indeed he accounted them prejudicial, so far from an advantage, that they were a damage to him, looking for Salvation by Christ alone, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 21.31. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.30. Col. 2.2.</ns0:note> the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Compar'd with the surpassing worth, and excellency in the fiducial, experimental (as is plain from what follows) knowledge of Jesus Christ in his person, Offi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, and benefits wherein an eye of faith can discern transcen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent mysteries, <ns0:hi>Is.</ns0:hi> 53.11. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 17.3. 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.20. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.16. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.12. to be ador'd by the sincere servants of so ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cellent a Lord, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 5.30, 33. to have an interest in whom, and to enjoy whom every thing besides is despicable.</ns0:note>: for whom I have suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fered the loss of all things <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>For whom</ns0:hi> (he adds) he did not onely account them loss (as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7.) in his judgment and readiness to loose them, but he actually sustained the loss of them, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 20.23. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.13. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.23, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> as to any plea for his acceptance, he suffered them all to go in this case, which he could not do till God of his rich and insuperable grace, wrought this resolution in him, by his holy Spirit, then he willingly did it.</ns0:note>, and do count them but dung <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Yea and upon a right sta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting of the accounts he reckon'd he was no loo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>er by the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />change, in that he did esteem them in a just balance compa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring spiritual things with spiritual, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.13. in point of trust, those excellent things, with an excellent Christ<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to be no better than dung (as we with the <ns0:hi>Syriac</ns0:hi> and others trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />late the word) or Dogs-meat, refuse cast to the Dogs, with others (and might agree with the gust of those, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. whom he calls Dogs, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 15.26. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 7.28.) Those much conversant in <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Authours do criticize largely upon the word, which is acknowledg'd on all hands to import things if not loath<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />some, yet vile, and contemptible, as Chaff, or <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and so not absolutely but in their respect, did <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> account all things in comparison of Christ, even our good works proceeding from an heart sanctified but in part; he doth not mean of the substance, but quality of the trust or merit placed in them, not in themselves, but in regard of confidence in them, as to pardon and acceptance with God: not in point of sanctification, but justification, the Apostle is here speaking to. So to rely up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on them would not onely comparatively, but positively be grea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />test loss, as keeping from Christ, who is the greatest gain; for which the loss of all beside was to be sustained.</ns0:note>, that I may win Christ <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That he might gain him, and be assured of an interest in him, whom he had a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove describ'd in his state of humiliation and exaltation, and en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joy Communion with him, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 11.28. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 14.26, 33. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.6. 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.12. of whom he would receive more, and for whom he would do more, aiming at the making of Christ himself his own, by some kind of propriety, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.30.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">As he had reckon'd and rated when he was first wrought upon to entertain Christ, so at present he did not alter his judgment, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>, pass'd through perils for the name of Christ. He remarka<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:498" />9 And be found in him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">A learned interpreter reads it actively, and may find, or recover in him, all my losses. But following our own trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation. By winning of Christ, the Apostle doth not onely mean the profession of the faith of the Gospel but his union with Christ, and participation of him, which in the judgment of the all seeing God, will answer all damages, when a man comes to stand in judgment at his tribunal here or hereafter, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.1. this being the onely course can be taken to be found of him in peace at the last, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.14. for out of him is to be under the curse, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.10. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.3, 12, 13. It is necessary therefore that a man be implanted into him who in his priestly Office acted in our name towards God, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 5.1. & 10.7. and that he abide in him, our head, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6.56. & 15.4. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5.30. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.6, 7. 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.12. and not be found in himself.</ns0:note>, not having mine own righteousness <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">That we might more fully understand his meaning of <ns0:hi>being found in Christ.</ns0:hi> He defines it negatively, and positively, by distinguishing of a <ns0:hi>twofold</ns0:hi> righteousness, supposing one necessary to his acceptance with God 1. inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rent within him, which he called his <ns0:hi>own,</ns0:hi> as being personally perform'd by him.</ns0:note>, which is of the law <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Who describes it to be in a conformi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty to the law, and the righteousness which the law requires, and those works of it, which if a man do, loving God withall his heart, he shall live in them, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.13. & 3.27, 28. & 10.5. He makes no distinction of any works done by him before or after conversion, but declares he dare not adventure to be found in any personal inherent righteousness of his <ns0:hi>own,</ns0:hi> as to the special end of his justification before God, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.10, 11, 12. But 2. he stays upon a righteousness without him, which is <ns0:hi>not his own</ns0:hi> by any acquisition of his, but the righteousness of another, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 3.5, 6, 7.</ns0:note>, but that which is through the faith of Christ <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> of Christ, without which he would not be found, and in which he would be found, <ns0:hi>i. e. that which is through the faith of Christ,</ns0:hi> having him for its ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ject, which he doth elsewhere oppose to the deeds of the law, or works of righteousness that he had done, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.28. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.16. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 3.5. as he doth <ns0:hi>believing</ns0:hi> unto <ns0:hi>doing,</ns0:hi> which de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scribe these two sorts of righteousness, in the one of which he would be found at his Tryal for justification, in the other he would not, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.17. & 10.5, 10, 11. hence,</ns0:note>, the righteousness which is of God by faith <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He doth by the following expression signifie more clearly the righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness he stays himself upon, and wherein he would be found at God's tribunal, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the same righteousness, which <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> had an Eye upon (typified by the Ark) when by preparing an Ark, he became heir of the righteousness which is by faith, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.7. <ns0:hi>the righteousness which is of God by Faith,</ns0:hi> not his own, but counted unto him for righteousness, as unto <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> who believed God, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.4. as unto <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> unto whom God imputed righteousness without works, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.6. They did goe about to mingle the Law and the Gospel, to join <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> with Christ for Justificati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4, <ns0:hi>&c. Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.21. and so undervalue redemption from the curse, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.13 & 5.2, 4. in <ns0:hi>special</ns0:hi> these <ns0:hi>Epi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cureans</ns0:hi> (as should seem they were by the following cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />racter, rather than real Christians) might rightly be called Enemies, because they did seem by their sensuality to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />store the Kingdom to those whom Christ had on his Cross openly spoil'd of it, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.15. that they might gratifie the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> in urging the necessity of Circumcision, so un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dermining the vertue and merit of Christ's Passion, de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />faming the end of it, as the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> did him in it, and in times of Tryal avoid persecution, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.12, 14. they shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed themselves by interpretation really to be Enemies to Christ Crucified, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.23, 24. & 2.2.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Whose end <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> destruction <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">(3) Their condition will at last be miserable as he had limited above, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.28. of their being under the dismal token of perdition, their end will be according to their works, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.15.                   <ns0:hi>whose</ns0:hi> glory <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in their shame <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Yea, they boast of those things whereof they ought to be ashamed, thinking it reputation they have got many to imitate them, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.44. & 12.43.                <ns0:p n="20">20 For our conversation is in heaven <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He here adds a further reason why he would have them to be fellow-followers of him, and such like as he, because though they were not already in Heaven, yet their Citizen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship was there, the privileges of that City did belong to them, who according to the Municipal Laws of that Cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poration (which cannot lose its Charter or be discor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />porated) whereof they were free Denizons, made it their business to demean themselves with minds above the earth, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.27. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.18. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.6. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.1. accounting no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing inconvenient to any one of them, which was for the advantage of the whole community, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.42. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.2. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.14. they <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>et their affections on things above.</ns0:note>, from whence also we * look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And reason good, for from thence or from that place, in the Heavens, or Heaven, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 1.11. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.7. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.10. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.8. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 2.13.                <ns0:p n="21">21 Who shall change our vile <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Who shall transform the body of our humility, or our lowliness, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> of low-brought body, the singular for the plural, our humble and mean bodies, which depend upon and are beholding to our eating and drinking, and the actions which follow thereupon, that do humble and lower them, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 1.48. now it may be languishing with pains, sickness and many infirmities, perhaps cooped up in a noisome, Prison, and it may be an unclean dungeon, sown in dishonour and weakness in the grave, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.43.</ns0:note> body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">That they may be conform'd to Christ's incorruptible, impassible and im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mortal body and so glorious, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.51, 52, 53. in their proportion agreeing with the blessed body of our Lord when he shall appear, 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.1, 2, 3. and they shall see him with the Eyes of their bodies made like unto his, <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 19.26, 27. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3, 4. not in equality, but onely in respect of the same qualities that his body hath, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.51, 52, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.17. A conformity agreeable to that of head and members, that mark as the Sun is the fountain of all that glory, which the Stars have, so shall our Lord and Saviour Christ's glory be of all our glory, <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 12.3. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 16.27. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.40, 41. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.14. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 21.11.23. But we must not imagine that our bodies shall be rais'd to the same height and degree of glory that his is: and therefore in regard of that power and ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jesty which is included in the body of Christ from the hyposta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tical union, our bodies will not be conformable, or made like to his; but in glory which he obtain'd from his Resurrection. For the body of Christ may be considered either 1. In its na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, and so there will be an agreement 'twixt the bodies of Saints and Christ's body, or 2.
